Console demo for keys and usage
Quickstart sample app and pilot scoping
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Alex from Redwood, AE. We also have Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Jordan (Nova): Good, thanks. Jordan here, engineering lead. Maya and Carlos from infra/security are on.
[00:14] Priya (Redwood): Hi all, quick agenda: we want to run through the SDK quickstarts — Python and TypeScript, show auth patterns, environment setup, and then walk through a minimal integration you can use for the pilot.
[00:26] Maya (Nova): Sounds good. We're mostly interested in embeddings and chat generation endpoints. Latency is a big piece for us.
[00:32] Alex (Redwood): Great, we'll cover that. Quick callouts: we'll point you to the console to create API keys and show the service-account flow for dedicated/private installs.
[00:40] Jordan: Perfect. Also we'll need to understand what data flows out — egress, logs, and retention.
[00:45] Carlos (Nova Security): Yes, SOC2 and KMS support are must haves — and audit logs.
[00:52] Priya: Totally. We'll show where audit logs live in the console and how to wire a KMS for envelope encryption.
[00:58] Alex: Ok jumping into the SDK. Priya, do you want to share the quickstart?
[01:02] Priya: Yep starting screen share. I'll paste the GitHub quickstart link in chat — it's a minimal app with both Python and TypeScript examples. The install section: pip install redwood-sdk (note: internal package name in quickstart may show as redwood-infer or redwood-sdk depending on release).
[01:20] [Speaker 1]: the transcript generator misheard a package name there, but the repo link is correct.
[01:25] Priya: For Node: npm i @redwood/inference or yarn add @redwood/inference. In both languages auth is via REDWOOD_API_KEY env var for hosted. For Dedicated/Private we support service accounts and SSO tokens.
[01:40] Jordan: Can you show a quick Python snippet for text generation and streaming?
[01:44] Priya: Sure. Example: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.chat.create(model='vicuna-13b', messages=[{'role':'user','content':'Summarize our Q4 sales notes'}]) — that's the sync call. For streaming we use client.chat.stream(...). The callback model yields partial tokens.
[02:08] Maya: Any rate-limits or default timeouts in the SDK?
[02:11] Priya: Default per-request timeout is 30s in the SDK but configurable. We also include built-in retry/backoff. There are client-side batching helpers for embeddings to reduce per-request overhead.
[02:25] Alex: A note about models: our console shows recommended models per workload, and Optimize suggests quantization and batching settings. We'll share that view.
[02:33] Jordan: How do we handle service account auth for Dedicated? We can't use long-lived API keys.
[02:38] Priya: For Dedicated or Private there's a service account flow: you mint a short-lived JWT from your internal identity provider (OIDC) and exchange it at the control plane for a scoped token, or we can integrate SAML/SSO to issue machine tokens. The quickstart repo has a small helper script for exchanges.
[02:56] Carlos: Is there support for rotating keys and KMS wrapping? We need HSM-backed key management for prod.
[03:02] Priya: Yes. We integrate with customer KMS—both AWS KMS and GCP KMS supported, and for on-prem HSM we have a plug-in. In the console you can set an envelope key. Audit logs will show key usage events.
[03:16] Maya: Ok good. For environment setup, is it just REDWOOD_API_KEY or do we need additional env vars?
[03:21] Priya: For hosted: REDWOOD_API_KEY and optional REDWOOD_BASE_URL if you're pointing at a region endpoint. For Dedicated: REDWOOD_TOKEN and REDWOOD_CLUSTER_ID or a local socket for private on-prem. The repo README enumerates them.
[03:36] Jordan: Can you show the Node example for embeddings? We plan to compute product embeddings for search.
[03:40] Priya: Sure — TypeScript snippet: import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const emb = await client.embeddings.create({model: 's-embedding-small', input: ['product title', 'product description']}); The SDK returns a payload with embedding vectors and request metadata (latency, tokens).
[03:58] Jordan: Nice. How about streaming embeddings or batching?
[04:02] Priya: Embeddings are typically batched; we provide a batch helper that will chunk inputs and parallelize to meet throughput targets. No streaming for embeddings; streaming is for generation/chat.
[04:12] Maya: What's the typical per-embedding latency and cost?
[04:15] Alex: Depends on model and whether you use quantized variants. Our Optimize product will recommend a model and quantization profile for embedding workloads. We'll share a spreadsheet with cost estimates based on your QPS.
[04:26] Jordan: Great. Could you walk through console to create an API key and where to find usage metrics?
[04:30] Priya: Switching tabs — console view. (screen share) Top right -> API Keys -> Create Key -> pick scope: read/write or embeddings-only. You can label keys per environment. Usage metrics are per-key and per-route in the Observability -> Usage tab.
[04:46] Carlos: Do audit logs include raw request bodies? We need to ensure sensitive PII is not captured unless explicitly requested.
[04:53] Priya: By default logs capture metadata (timestamps, model, tokens, latency, key id) but not full request text — unless you enable debug logging. For customers who want full-recording we support redaction rules and can route logs to their S3 for retention/compliance.
[05:12] Jordan: Ok. For the quickstart — what's the fastest way to get a dev environment running?
[05:16] Priya: Steps: 1) Clone quickstart repo, 2) npm install or pip install -r requirements, 3) set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env, 4) run sample app (python app.py or npm start). We'll paste commands in chat now.
[05:30] [00:05:30] Priya pastes commands in chat: git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts.git 
cd quickstarts/sdk-basic 
python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate 
pip install -r requirements.txt 
export REDWOOD_API_KEY="<key>" 
python app.py
[05:52] Maya: Do you support running locally with a dev proxy? We have a staging network pattern where egress is locked down.
[05:57] Priya: Yes, the SDK supports a REDWOOD_BASE_URL env var so you can proxy through your internal gateway; for strict staging we often run a sidecar that handles token exchange.
[06:08] Jordan: What about streaming on mobile or web — do you have a recommended pattern for TypeScript to pipe chunks to UI?
[06:13] Priya: For browser apps we recommend using our streaming WebSocket/Server-Sent-Events endpoint alongside the Node SDK to pre-sanitize and watermark content. The TypeScript client has an example using EventSource to append tokens to the DOM as they arrive.
[06:29] Jordan: Great. Can we run a small benchmark during the pilot to validate P99 latency?
[06:33] Alex: Absolutely. Priya can run a small bench on a sample payload and share results; for more rigorous tests we can provide a balancer script.
[06:39] Priya: I'll need a sample payload and expected QPS; I'll spin up a quick test and share results in the repo.
[06:45] Carlos: Security question — where do logs live for Private deployments? We need them to egress to our SIEM.
[06:51] Priya: In Private you control the logging sink; we can push audit logs to your S3/GCS or directly to Splunk via an agent. The control plane will have an admin view if you opt-in; otherwise logs stay within your VPC.
[07:05] Jordan: On the SDK topic: do we get typed responses for TS? Does the client surface request/response types?
[07:09] Priya: Yes, the TypeScript client ships with full types for request/response shapes, including helpful discriminated unions for message roles and tool calls.
[07:18] Maya: Regarding model versions: can we pin model versions in requests? We need determinism for evaluations.
[07:23] Priya: You can pin both model version and a quantization profile in the request. We also have per-route pinning in the console so you can set a default for a service.
[07:33] Jordan: Are there SDK metrics emitted for telemetry? Our infra team wants to capture SDK-level metrics for alerting.
[07:39] Priya: The SDK exposes hooks for metrics; it ships with lightweight metrics collectors that export Prometheus counters (latency histograms, success/fail counts) and a span per request that can be forwarded to your tracing backend.
[07:54] Alex: Quick note about error handling — we have typed errors for rate limit, capacity fallbacks, and model-mismatch. The SDK can auto-fallback to a cheaper model when latency SLOs are breached if you enable auto-fallback policies.
[08:10] Jordan: That fallback behavior — is it client-side or server-side? We want deterministic behavior.
[08:14] Priya: It's server-side routing policy. You can signal a route-level policy to prefer latency or cost; the control plane will pick a compatible variant. Client-side you can also implement a retry to a different model.
[08:28] Maya: Ok, can we talk about cost controls — token caps per key?
[08:32] Alex: Yes, per-key quotas and spend alerts. We also have per-route budget controls in the console. We'll send screenshots.
[08:41] [00:08:41] Jordan: Any known pitfalls for onboarding?
[08:44] Priya: Common gotchas: auth env var not set, local firewall blocking streaming endpoints, and forgetting to set model/quantization profiles. Quickstart README has a checklist.
[08:56] Carlos: One more security: do you support VPC Service Controls or private service connect?
[09:01] Priya: For Private deployments yes; for Hosted we support region-restricted endpoints and peering for Dedicated. We can discuss network topology with your cloud team during the POC kickoff.
[09:13] Alex: Ok let's recap next steps. Alex will send the quickstart repo link, pricing guidance, and console screenshots; Priya will run a small benchmark given sample payload and expected QPS; Jordan will confirm pilot scope and any network constraints.
[09:28] Jordan: Sounds good. Anything else?
[09:30] Maya: Could you also include sample code for batch embeddings and a Node streaming example?
[09:35] Priya: Yes I'll add both to the repo.
[09:37] Carlos: And include the security docs (SOC2, KMS integrations, audit log format).
[09:42] Alex: We'll attach the security pack and a short checklist for compliance.
[09:46] Jordan: Thanks everyone, look forward to the POC.
[09:49] Alex: Thanks — we'll follow up via email with links and schedule the technical kickoff.
[09:52] [END]
notes: Customer interested in embeddings + chat with focus on latency. Security requires KMS/HSM, audit logs, and key rotation. Pilot to validate P99 latency and cost tradeoffs. SE to run small benchmark; AE to share quickstart and security pack.
